description:
I am an ML engineer working with PyTorch and Python. We are building ARES-MAP: an interactive, web-based 3D tactical mission planner for astronauts on Mars (Jezero Crater). We use real NASA HiRISE terrain and an ML backend predicting dynamic hazards (temperature, dust storms, radiation) to generate safe EVA routes.

Looking for:

• Godot 4 / 3D Developer (WebGL, shaders, atmospheric fog)

• Frontend Web Dev (interactive portal, UI/UX)

Clear architecture is ready—let's build a winning project!
summary:
ARES-MAP (Autonomous Reconnaissance & EVA Surface Mapping) is an interactive 3D surface hazard map and route planner built to help astronauts plan safer Marswalks in Jezero Crater.

While existing tools like JPL Mars Trek are built for regional and global exploration, an astronaut heading out on foot needs localized, hour-by-hour conditions for a single excursion. ARES-MAP brings together five NASA data layers: 1-meter-per-pixel MRO HiRISE elevation and optical imagery of Jezero's western delta, Perseverance MEDA weather and wind logs, and Curiosity RAD radiation readings. Given any Martian day and hour, our PyTorch forecast model and FastAPI backend pack four risk scores (cold, dust, and radiation) into one map layered onto 3D terrain for obstacle-avoiding route planning.

On Mars, temperatures drop below -90°C, dust cuts visibility, and pressurized suits risk tipping on steep crater walls. Turning raw rover and orbiter data into one clear walking map keeps crews safer and frees them to focus on field science.
details:
What It Does and How It Works

ARES-MAP (Autonomous Reconnaissance & EVA Surface Mapping) turns raw NASA orbiter and rover archives into an interactive 3D Marswalk planner for Jezero Crater's western delta (18.38°N, 77.58°E). Instead of looking at a static map from orbit, an astronaut or mission planner picks any Martian day (Sol) and hour of the day to see what surface conditions will actually look like on the ground.

Behind the scenes, a PyTorch neural network (`MarsEnvMLP`), trained on 2,511 aligned records from Perseverance's MEDA weather station and Curiosity's RAD radiation detector, predicts ground and air temperatures, dust optical depth and radiation dose rate. Our FastAPI server combines that forecast with 1-meter-per-pixel MRO HiRISE elevation and sky-exposure geometry to generate three environmental hazard layers: Thermal Cold (Red, highlighting sub-zero shadowed slopes and cold basins), Dust & Visibility (Green, tracking wind-blown dust settling in low terrain), and Cosmic Radiation (Purple, comparing exposed ridges against sheltered crater walls). The 3D viewer drapes these layers over displaced terrain meshes and uses A* pathfinding to suggest safer routes between science stops.

Benefits and Intended Impact

Existing tools like JPL Mars Trek and the USGS-NASA Planetary Geologic Mapping Program excel at regional and global views, but crews heading out for a four-hour walk need local, hour-by-hour context. ARES-MAP bridges that gap for habitat pre-EVA briefings, carried field tablets, or future visor HUDs. By showing where pre-dawn temperatures plunge past -90°C, where wind cuts visibility, and where terrain naturally shields against cosmic rays, the tool helps astronauts conserve suit battery power, limit radiation exposure, and spend more time doing high-value field science on Jezero's ancient delta mudstones and rim carbonates.

Tools, Languages, Data, and Software Used

Backend & Machine Learning: Python, PyTorch, FastAPI, NumPy, Pandas, SciPy, Rasterio, and Pillow.

3D & Web Frontend: HTML5, CSS, JavaScript, Godot 4 (for the interactive 3D terrain and route explorer), glTF (`.glb`) / Wavefront (`.obj`) mesh export pipelines, 4096×4096 16-bit heightmaps, and WebGL 2 shader integration.

NASA Data Sources: MRO HiRISE stereo DTM (`DTEEC_045994_1985_046060_1985_U01.IMG`) and orthophoto (`ESP_046060_1985_RED_C_01_ORTHO.JP2`) covering 4.14 × 4.14 km (alongside a 45 × 45 km procedural full-crater model), NASA PDS4 Perseverance MEDA (`CAL_TIRS`, `DER_PS`, `DER_WS` across 25 sols), and NASA PDS3 Curiosity RAD (`MSL-M-RAD-3-RDR-V1.0`, 1,370 dose records).

Creativity and Factors We Considered

A major design challenge was keeping 3D rendering fast enough for an everyday browser without sacrificing environmental detail. Rather than streaming bulky climate grids every time the user inputs a date and time, our backend packs all live hazard scores into a single lightweight RGB PNG texture that GPU shaders unpack in real time (taking ~23 ms to synthesize at 256×256).

We also accounted for messy real-world rover constraints. Because Perseverance's wind sensors were damaged after Sol 315, we fit seasonal-diurnal harmonics and modeled wind direction as sine/cosine components to avoid 0°/360° angle-wrap errors. We also factored in how Martian CO2 surface pressure shields against cosmic radiation, how cold air pools in low basins before dawn, and how blowing dust reduces visibility for buddy teams working away from the habitat.
